controversies/scripture-and-slavery/summ: Christians for centuries tolerated and often defended slavery; from the late 18th century Quakers, evangelicals, Methodists and Black Christians led the movement to abolish it, while Southern theologians defended it from Scripture. The debate tore American churches apart and remains a test case for biblical interpretation.
controversies/scripture-and-slavery/side: God made of one blood all nations; every person bears his image. Scripture condemns manstealing with death, and the gospel declares that in Christ there is neither bond nor free. The regulations of ancient servitude no more endorse American chattel slavery than the laws on divorce endorse divorce. We cannot claim to love our neighbour while owning him.
(Historically raised) explicit regulation of slavery in Scripture

(Reconstructed historically, not endorsed.) Its defenders claimed that the patriarchs held slaves, Moses regulated slavery, Jesus never condemned it and Paul told slaves to obey, so to call slaveholding sin was to correct God’s Word by human sentiment. Virtually all churches now regard this argument as a grave misuse of Scripture.
Race-based chattel slavery unlike Hebrew servitude
controversies/scripture-and-slavery/time: Gregory of Nyssa condemns slaveholding in his Fourth Homily on Ecclesiastes.
Dum Diversas authorises Portuguese enslavement of "Saracens and pagans".
Valladolid debate on the rights of indigenous Americans.
Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade founded in London.
Gregory XVI condemns the slave trade (In Supremo Apostolatus).
Southern Baptist Convention founded after the slavery split; Douglass’ Narrative published.
Thirteenth Amendment abolishes slavery in the United States.
Brazil abolishes slavery (Lei Áurea), the last in the Americas.
Southern Baptist Convention resolution repents of its defence of slavery and racism.
controversies/scripture-and-slavery/reso: Settled morally: all major churches now condemn slavery as sin and many have formally repented of past complicity. Resolved politically by abolition laws and, in the US, a civil war. Its legacies (racism, segregated churches, hermeneutical debates) remain contested.
controversies/scripture-and-slavery/cons: Split major American denominations and contributed to the Civil War.
Gave rise to independent Black churches (AME, AME Zion, National Baptist Convention).
Became a paradigm case in debates about biblical interpretation and moral development.
controversies/church-and-state/question: Should the Church be allied with, separate from, or prophetic toward the state?
controversies/church-and-state/title: Church and state: Christendom, two kingdoms, separation and resistance
controversies/church-and-state/summary: Since Constantine, Christians have debated whether a Christian state should support the true faith, how spiritual and temporal powers relate, whether the Church should withdraw from coercive politics, and when it must resist. Modern debates over Christian nationalism, liberation and religious liberty continue the argument.
controversies/church-and-state/sides/0/s: Christ is Lord of nations as well as souls. A Christian ruler should protect the Church, honour God’s law and nurture a Christian people, while the Church sanctifies and counsels rulers. This partnership gave the world Byzantium, Ethiopia and the medieval West.
controversies/church-and-state/sides/1/s: God rules the world with two hands. The gospel creates faith and cannot be forced; the sword restrains evil and cannot save. Keep them distinct, and Christians can serve faithfully as citizens and officials without confusing the state with the Church.
controversies/church-and-state/sides/1/a: Render to Caesar and to God
controversies/church-and-state/sides/2/s: The Church is a voluntary fellowship that cannot be created by law. Christendom made persecutors of Christians. Let the Church be the Church: free from the state, refusing its sword, and witnessing to Christ’s kingdom by its life.
controversies/church-and-state/sides/3/s: When the state becomes an idol or an oppressor, the Church must say "we ought to obey God rather than men". At Barmen, in Birmingham, in San Salvador and Soweto, Christians confessed Christ’s lordship against racial, national and economic idols and stood with the oppressed.
controversies/church-and-state/sides/4/s: (As its advocates put it.) Every nation has a public faith; ours should be Christian. Christians should shape laws and culture in line with God’s will and the nation’s Christian heritage rather than surrender the public square to secularism.
controversies/church-and-state/timeline/: Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state religion.
Boniface VIII’s Unam Sanctam asserts papal supremacy over temporal power.
Peace of Augsburg: cuius regio, eius religio.
US First Amendment forbids an established church.
Vatican II’s Dignitatis Humanae affirms religious liberty.
Orthodox theologians’ Declaration on the "Russian World" teaching.
controversies/church-and-state/resolutio: Most churches now accept religious liberty and some form of church–state distinction (Catholic Church since Vatican II); established churches persist in some countries; debates over Christian nationalism, religious liberty and prophetic engagement remain intense worldwide.
controversies/church-and-state/consequen: Shaped the political history of Europe, the Americas, Byzantium, Russia and Ethiopia.
Produced modern religious liberty and separation of church and state.
Continues to shape elections, wars and human-rights struggles.
controversies/new-prophecy-controversy/q: Can new prophecy add to the apostolic faith?
controversies/new-prophecy-controversy/s: In 2nd-century Phrygia, Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla claimed the Paraclete was speaking through them with new disciplines and an imminent end. The resulting conflict produced the first recorded church synods and helped define how the Church tests prophecy and relates it to Scripture and bishops.

Christ promised the Paraclete would lead us into all truth. The same Spirit who spoke through Agabus and Philip’s daughters now speaks through our prophets, not to change the faith but to call a lax Church to the discipline and courage the last days require. The bishops who silence the Spirit are quenching what Paul told us not to quench.
Moral seriousness and readiness for martyrdom
Ecstatic first-person prophecy differs from biblical prophecy

We do not despise prophecy; Irenaeus rejoices that brothers in the Church prophesy. But true prophets speak with self-control, agree with the apostolic rule of faith, and are tested by the whole Church. A prophecy that claims to be the Paraclete himself, abandons sober speech, makes predictions that fail and sets itself above the apostolic tradition is not from the Spirit of Christ.
Spirits of prophets are subject to prophets (1 Cor 14:32)
Risk of quenching the Spirit and institutionalising the Church
controversies/new-prophecy-controversy/t: Montanus begins prophesying at Ardabau in Phrygia (date per Epiphanius; Eusebius suggests c.172).
Synods in Asia Minor examine and excommunicate the New Prophecy; the martyrs of Lyon write to Rome counselling peace.
After initial sympathy, Roman bishops reject the New Prophecy.
Tertullian in Carthage embraces the New Prophecy.
Tertullian’s Against Praxeas accuses Praxeas of driving out the Paraclete at Rome.
Under Justinian, John of Ephesus destroys the Montanist shrine and relics at Pepuza.
controversies/new-prophecy-controversy/r: The catholic Church excommunicated the New Prophecy, which survived as a separate church in Phrygia and North Africa (Tertullianists) until the 6th century. The episode strengthened episcopal authority, the closing of the canon and caution toward ecstatic prophecy.
controversies/new-prophecy-controversy/c: First recorded church synods held to settle a doctrinal question.
Contributed to the sense that revelation ended with the apostles and to the formation of the New Testament canon.
Set a pattern of suspicion toward ecstatic prophecy and female prophetic leadership.
controversies/are-the-miraculous-gifts-f: Are the miraculous gifts of the Spirit for today?
Cessationism versus continuationism

Do prophecy, tongues, healing and miracles continue in the Church, or did they cease with the apostles? The question, sharpened by the Reformation and then by the rise of Pentecostalism, divides evangelicals and shapes worship, mission and pastoral practice worldwide.
Cessationist

The sign-gifts were the credentials of the apostles and the scaffolding of a Church still receiving revelation. Once the foundation was laid and Scripture completed, the scaffolding came down. God still heals in answer to prayer, but to claim ongoing prophecy is to threaten the sufficiency of Scripture, and history shows how often such claims lead people astray.
Signs of an apostle (2 Cor 12:12)
Foundation of apostles and prophets (Eph 2:20)
Sufficiency of Scripture
Historical decline of the gifts
No text sets an end-date before Christ’s return
Augustine and others reported continuing miracles
Ephesians 2:20
Hebrews 2:3–4
2 Corinthians 12:12
Continuationist (open but cautious)

Paul told the Corinthians to desire spiritual gifts and not to forbid tongues, and said these gifts would end only when we see Christ face to face. Prophecy today is not Scripture: it is weighed and tested. The Church should neither despise prophecy nor believe every spirit.
1 Corinthians 13:10 refers to the eschaton
Gifts are for the common good of every church
Patristic and modern reports of miracles
Category of fallible prophecy is novel
Abuses and false prophecy
1 Corinthians 12:7; 14:1, 39
1 Thessalonians 5:19–21
Pentecostal (initial evidence)

The promise is "to you and to your children and to all that are afar off". Pentecost was not a one-off but the pattern: believers are baptised in the Spirit for power to witness, and the Bible evidence is speaking in tongues. The explosive growth of Spirit-filled churches across the world is the Lord confirming the word with signs following.
Pattern of Acts 2, 10, 19
Promise of Acts 2:39
Missionary empowerment
"Do all speak with tongues?" (1 Cor 12:30)
Narrative is not normative
Pentecost: tongues and prophecy at the Church’s birth.
The New Prophecy controversy raises the question of continuing prophecy.
Chrysostom notes that the Corinthian gifts no longer occur.
Augustine records contemporary healings (City of God 22.8).
Calvin argues that new miracles are not needed to confirm the gospel.
Welsh revival heightens expectation of a new Pentecost.
Azusa Street revival launches global Pentecostalism.
Warfield’s Counterfeit Miracles.
Charismatic renewal reaches the historic denominations.
Toronto Blessing provokes fierce debate over manifestations.
Grudem’s Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views.
John MacArthur’s Strange Fire conference attacks the charismatic movement; widespread continuationist rebuttals follow.
Asbury revival reopens discussion of revival without manifestations.

Unresolved. Pentecostal, charismatic and most Global South churches are continuationist; Catholic and Orthodox churches affirm charisms within sacramental order; confessional Reformed and some Baptist churches remain cessationist; many evangelical networks treat the question as secondary.
Defines denominational boundaries and church-planting networks.
Shapes worship style, healing ministry and deliverance practice worldwide.
Drives a large apologetic and scholarly literature on miracles.
